title: Improved analysis and evaluation of real-time semaphore protocols for P-FP scheduling

extraction.paper_name: Improved Analysis and Evaluation of Real-Time Semaphore Protocols for P-FP Scheduling
extraction.paper_description: This paper introduces a new linear-programming-based blocking analysis technique for suspension-based multiprocessor real-time locking protocols under partitioned fixed-priority (P-FP) scheduling. It compares four protocols (MPCP, FMLP+, DPCP, DFLP) and provides significantly less pessimistic blocking bounds than prior ad-hoc approaches, leading to improved schedulability analysis.

formal_description.statement: A real-time workload consists of n sporadic tasks tau = {tau_1, ..., tau_n} scheduled on m identical processors P_1, ..., P_m. For each task tau_i: e_i is its worst-case execution cost, p_i is its period, J_i denotes a job of tau_i. A task's utilization is u_i = e_i / p_i. J_i is pending from its release until it completes. tau_i's worst-case response time r_i denotes the maximum duration that any J_i remains pending. We assume implicit deadlines (r_i <= p_i).

variables.e_i: worst-case execution cost of task tau_i
variables.r_i: worst-case response time of task tau_i

formal_description.conclusion: Defines fundamental parameters for tasks and the system.

informal_sketch.intuition: This defines the basic building blocks of our real-time system: tasks, their execution requirements, how often they run, and how long they can take to finish. Utilization tells us how much of a single processor a task demands.
steps: A task tau_i needs e_i time to execute.
It arrives every p_i time units (at most).
Its utilization u_i is simply e_i / p_i, representing its CPU demand ratio.
r_i is the longest time from release to completion for any of its jobs.
Implicit deadlines mean a task must finish within its period (r_i <= p_i).
key_insights: Tasks are sporadic, meaning minimum inter-arrival time is p_i.
Utilization is a key metric for processor load.
Response time is the ultimate measure of task performance against its deadline.

formal_description.statement: Besides the m processors, tasks share n_r serially-reusable resources q_1, ..., q_nr. N_i_q denotes the maximum number of times that any job J_i accesses resource q. L_i_q denotes tau_i's maximum critical section length, i.e., the maximum time that any J_i uses q as part of a single access (L_i_q = 0 if N_i_q = 0). Jobs request and hold at most one resource at any time.

variables.N_i_q: maximum number of accesses by job J_i to resource q
variables.L_i_q: maximum critical section length for resource q by task tau_i

assumptions: Jobs release all resources before completion
Jobs request and hold at most one resource at any time
formal_description.conclusion: Defines parameters related to shared resources and their usage by tasks.

informal_sketch.intuition: This describes how tasks interact with shared resources. N_i_q tells us how many times a task needs a resource, and L_i_q tells us how long it holds that resource each time. These are crucial for calculating blocking.
steps: Identify the total number of shared resources, n_r.
For each task tau_i and resource q, determine N_i_q, the maximum number of times tau_i will access q.
For each task tau_i and resource q, determine L_i_q, the maximum duration of a single critical section for q by tau_i.
If tau_i never accesses q, then N_i_q = 0 and L_i_q = 0.
key_insights: Resource usage is quantified by frequency (N_i_q) and duration (L_i_q).
These parameters directly influence potential blocking times.

formal_description.statement: Under P-FP scheduling, each task has a unique, fixed base priority, and is statically assigned to one of the m processors; P_tau_i denotes tau_i's assigned processor. A priority inversion exists if a high-priority job J_i that should be scheduled is not scheduled (e.g., while waiting to acquire a lock). Formally, J_i incurs a priority inversion at time t if J_i is pending and neither J_i nor a higher-priority job are scheduled on processor P_tau_i at time t. Pi-blocking is the locking-related delay causing priority inversions. Pi-blocking is local (accounted for by b_l_i) when caused by critical sections executed on processor P_tau_i, and remote (accounted for by b_r_i) otherwise.

variables.b_l_i: bound on maximum local pi-blocking for task tau_i
variables.b_r_i: bound on maximum remote pi-blocking for task tau_i

assumptions: Tasks have unique, fixed base priorities
Tasks are statically assigned to processors
formal_description.conclusion: Defines priority inversion and categorizes pi-blocking into local and remote components, which are crucial for response time analysis.

informal_sketch.intuition: Priority inversion is when a high-priority task is ready to run but can't because a lower-priority task (or some other blocking mechanism) is holding it up. This delay is called pi-blocking. It's 'local' if the blocking happens on the task's own processor, and 'remote' if it's due to activity on another processor.
steps: Assign each task tau_i to a specific processor P_tau_i.
Assign a fixed priority to each task.
If a job J_i is ready to run on P_tau_i, but P_tau_i is busy with a lower-priority job or an agent, J_i experiences a priority inversion.
The duration of this inversion is pi-blocking.
Categorize pi-blocking as b_l_i if the blocking critical section is on P_tau_i, or b_r_i if it's on a different processor.
key_insights: Pi-blocking directly increases a task's response time.
Distinguishing local and remote blocking is essential for multiprocessor analysis, especially with distributed protocols.

formal_description.statement:
Whether a task set is schedulable under P-FP scheduling in the presence of locks (i.e., whether r_i <= p_i for each tau_i) is commonly determined using response-time analysis, by solving the following recurrence for each tau_i:

r_i = e_i + b_l_i + b_r_i + sum(for all tau_h where P_tau_h = P_tau_i AND h < i: ceil(r_i / p_h) * e_h)

variables.r_i: worst-case response time of task tau_i
variables.e_i: worst-case execution cost of task tau_i
variables.b_l_i: bound on maximum local pi-blocking for task tau_i
variables.b_r_i: bound on maximum remote pi-blocking for task tau_i
variables.h < i: task tau_h has higher priority than task tau_i

assumptions: Tasks are indexed in order of decreasing base priority (h < i implies tau_h has higher priority than tau_i)
formal_description.conclusion: Provides the fundamental recurrence relation to calculate the worst-case response time for a task under P-FP scheduling, considering execution, blocking, and higher-priority interference.

informal_sketch.intuition: A task's total response time is its own execution time, plus any time it's blocked by locks, plus any time it's preempted by higher-priority tasks on the same processor. This equation iteratively calculates that total time until it stabilizes.
steps: Start with an initial estimate for r_i (e.g., r_i = e_i).
For each task tau_i, calculate the total interference from higher-priority tasks (tau_h with h < i) on the same processor (P_tau_h = P_tau_i). This is `sum(ceil(r_i / p_h) * e_h)`.
Add tau_i's own execution time (e_i), local blocking (b_l_i), remote blocking (b_r_i), and the higher-priority interference.
Update r_i with this new value.
Repeat until r_i converges (stops changing) or exceeds p_i (indicating unschedulability).
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
import math

def calculate_response_time(task_i, task_set, b_l_i, b_r_i):
    r_i_current = task_i.e + b_l_i + b_r_i
    r_i_prev = 0

    while r_i_current != r_i_prev:
        r_i_prev = r_i_current
        interference = 0
        for task_h in task_set:
            # Higher priority and on the same processor
            if task_h.priority < task_i.priority and task_h.assigned_processor == task_i.assigned_processor:
                interference += math.ceil(r_i_prev / task_h.p) * task_h.e
        
        r_i_current = task_i.e + b_l_i + b_r_i + interference
        
        if r_i_current > task_i.p: # Check against deadline for early exit
            return r_i_current # Unschedulable

    return r_i_current
key_insights: This is an iterative fixed-point calculation.
Blocking terms (b_l_i, b_r_i) are critical inputs, and their accuracy directly impacts schedulability.
The `ceil(r_i / p_h)` term accounts for all jobs of higher-priority tasks that can interfere within `r_i`.

formal_description.statement:
Any locking-related pi-blocking coincides with one of the following kinds of delay:
1. Direct request delay: A job J_i requests a resource q that is currently not available. J_i waits for the lock holder to finish its critical section. Arises only via resources that J_i requests.
2. Indirect request delay: J_i waits for another job J_a to release a resource, and J_a is preempted by a third job J_b (or an agent acting on behalf of J_b), increasing J_i's total acquisition delay. Can arise due to shared resources that J_i never accesses.
3. Preemption delay: J_i is preempted by a priority-boosted, lower-priority job (or agent). Affects even tasks that do not access shared resources.
4. Agent execution delay: Time that a job is suspended under distributed locking protocols while an agent carries out its request. Not contention-related, but a source of delay and thus can cause priority inversions.

variables.J_a: job holding a resource J_i needs

formal_description.conclusion: Categorizes the different ways a job can be delayed due to locking mechanisms, forming the basis for blocking analysis.

informal_sketch.intuition: This breaks down the total blocking time into specific causes. Direct delay is waiting for a resource you asked for. Indirect delay is waiting for someone who's waiting for someone else. Preemption delay is being pushed off the CPU by a boosted lower-priority task. Agent delay is just the time spent waiting for a remote agent to do its work.
steps: If J_i needs resource q and it's busy, that's direct delay.
If J_i needs q, and the holder of q (J_a) is delayed by another job (J_b), that's indirect delay for J_i.
If J_i is running, but a lower-priority job gets a temporary priority boost (e.g., holding a lock) and preempts J_i, that's preemption delay.
In distributed protocols, if J_i sends a request to an agent and suspends, the time it waits for the agent to complete is agent execution delay.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
enum DelayType:
    DIRECT_REQUEST = 1
    INDIRECT_REQUEST = 2
    PREEMPTION = 3
    AGENT_EXECUTION = 4

def analyze_delay_cause(job_i, event):
    if event.type == 'resource_request' and event.resource.is_locked_by_other(job_i):
        return DelayType.DIRECT_REQUEST
    # ... similar logic for other types
key_insights: Each type of delay contributes to pi-blocking.
Understanding these distinctions is crucial for accurate modeling and bounding.

formal_description.statement: For a request R_x_q_v (the v-th request for q by jobs of tau_x while J_i is pending), let b_x_q_v_i denote the actual pi-blocking (of any kind) that J_i incurred due to the execution of R_x_q_v. The corresponding blocking fraction X_x_q_v = b_x_q_v_i / L_x_q relates the pi-blocking actually incurred by J_i to the maximum pi-blocking that R_x_q_v could have caused, where X_x_q_v is in [0, 1]. We analogously define X_D_x_q_v, X_I_x_q_v, and X_P_x_q_v to denote only the fraction of pi-blocking due to direct request delay, indirect request delay, and preemption delay, respectively.

variables.R_x_q_v: the v-th request for resource q by a job of task tau_x
variables.b_x_q_v_i: actual pi-blocking incurred by J_i due to R_x_q_v
variables.L_x_q: maximum critical section length for resource q by task tau_x
variables.X_D_x_q_v: direct delay blocking fraction for R_x_q_v
variables.X_I_x_q_v: indirect delay blocking fraction for R_x_q_v
variables.X_P_x_q_v: preemption delay blocking fraction for R_x_q_v

assumptions: L_x_q > 0 for any request R_x_q_v that causes blocking.
formal_description.conclusion: Introduces blocking fractions as variables to linearize the problem of bounding pi-blocking, allowing partial blocking to be modeled.

informal_sketch.intuition: Instead of just saying 'this request blocks', we quantify *how much* it blocks as a fraction of its maximum possible blocking duration. This allows us to model scenarios where critical sections only partially overlap or cause partial delays, making the analysis more precise.
steps: For any critical section R_x_q_v, its maximum duration is L_x_q.
If J_i is blocked by R_x_q_v for b_x_q_v_i time units, the blocking fraction X_x_q_v is b_x_q_v_i / L_x_q.
This fraction is between 0 (no blocking) and 1 (full blocking).
Separate fractions (X_D, X_I, X_P) are used for each type of delay.
key_insights: Blocking fractions convert complex, time-varying blocking into linear variables.
This linearization is key to using Linear Programming for blocking analysis.
Allows for fine-grained accounting of blocking, reducing pessimism.

formal_description.statement: R_P_k = {q | P_q = P_k} denotes the set of resources local to processor P_k. N_i_P_k = sum(for all q in R_P_k: N_i_q) denotes the maximum number of requests issued by J_i for resources in R_P_k.

variables.R_P_k: set of resources local to processor P_k
variables.N_i_P_k: maximum number of requests by J_i for resources on processor P_k
variables.N_i_q: maximum number of accesses by J_i to resource q

formal_description.conclusion: Defines helper sets and counts for resources grouped by processor, used in DFLP analysis.

informal_sketch.intuition: This groups resources by the processor they are 'local' to (where their agents run). N_i_P_k is simply the total number of times J_i needs *any* resource that is handled by processor P_k.
steps: For each processor P_k, identify all resources q for which P_q = P_k. This forms R_P_k.
For a task J_i, sum up all N_i_q for resources q in R_P_k to get N_i_P_k.
key_insights: Grouping resources by processor simplifies analysis for distributed protocols.
N_i_P_k represents the 'demand' J_i places on a specific synchronization processor.

results.identifier: Definition: Objective Function for Total PI-Blocking

formal_description.statement:
The total pi-blocking b_i for task tau_i is the sum of local and remote pi-blocking: b_i = b_l_i + b_r_i. These are defined as:

b_l_i = sum(for all q in lr_tau_i: N_i_q * L_i_q) + sum(for all tau_x in tau_i_prime: sum(for v from 1 to N_i_x_q: (X_D_x_q_v + X_I_x_q_v + X_P_x_q_v) * L_x_q))

b_r_i = sum(for all q in rr_tau_i: N_i_q * L_i_q) + sum(for all tau_x in tau_i_prime: sum(for v from 1 to N_i_x_q: (X_D_x_q_v + X_I_x_q_v + X_P_x_q_v) * L_x_q))

where:
- rr_tau_i = {q | P_q != P_tau_i} is the set of remote resources (w.r.t. tau_i).
- lr_tau_i = {q | P_q = P_tau_i} is the set of local resources (w.r.t. tau_i).
- tau_i_prime = tau \ {tau_i} is the set of all tasks except tau_i.
- N_i_x_q is the maximum number of requests for resource q issued by jobs of tau_x while J_i is pending, bounded by ceil((r_i + r_x) / p_x) * N_x_q.

variables.lr_tau_i: set of local resources for task tau_i
variables.rr_tau_i: set of remote resources for task tau_i
variables.N_i_q: max accesses by J_i to q
variables.L_i_q: max critical section length for q by J_i
variables.N_i_x_q: max requests by tau_x for q while J_i is pending
variables.L_x_q: max critical section length for q by tau_x
variables.N_x_q: max accesses by tau_x to q

assumptions: The execution cost e_i includes critical sections under shared-memory protocols, but not under distributed locking protocols (where critical sections may be executed remotely). This implies the N_i_q * L_i_q term for J_i's own requests is only for distributed protocols where J_i suspends for agent execution.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the objective function for the Linear Program, which aims to maximize the total pi-blocking for a task by summing up contributions from all potentially blocking critical sections, weighted by their blocking fractions.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is the formula we want to maximize to find the worst-case blocking. It sums up all possible blocking contributions. For each critical section (L_x_q) from other tasks (tau_x), we multiply its length by its blocking fraction (X_D + X_I + X_P). The N_i_x_q term estimates how many times a task tau_x can make requests while tau_i is active. The N_i_q * L_i_q term accounts for tau_i's own suspension time if it's a distributed protocol.
steps: Identify all resources local to tau_i's processor (lr_tau_i) and remote resources (rr_tau_i).
For each resource q, estimate N_i_x_q, the maximum number of times any other task tau_x can request q while tau_i is pending.
For each such request, define blocking fraction variables (X_D, X_I, X_P).
The total blocking b_i is the sum of all these (fraction * length) terms, plus tau_i's own agent execution delays if applicable.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
import math

def calculate_blocking_objective(task_i, task_set, resource_map, r_values, lp_solver_variables):
    b_l_i = 0
    b_r_i = 0

    # For distributed protocols, J_i's own requests contribute to agent execution delay
    # This part is implicitly handled by the LP for distributed protocols, 
    # but for shared-memory, e_i already includes it.
    # Assuming distributed protocol context for this formula:
    for q_id in task_i.lr_resources:
        b_l_i += task_i.N_q[q_id] * task_i.L_q[q_id]
    for q_id in task_i.rr_resources:
        b_r_i += task_i.N_q[q_id] * task_i.L_q[q_id]

    for task_x in task_set:
        if task_x.id == task_i.id: continue

        for q_id in resource_map.keys():
            if task_x.N_q.get(q_id, 0) == 0: continue
            
            # Calculate N_i_x_q coefficient for this (task_x, q_id) pair
            # This is the maximum number of requests by task_x for q that can potentially block task_i
            N_i_x_q_coeff = math.ceil((r_values[task_i.id] + r_values[task_x.id]) / task_x.p) * task_x.N_q[q_id]

            for v in range(1, int(N_i_x_q_coeff) + 1):
                # These X_D, X_I, X_P are LP variables, not fixed values
                # The LP solver will find values for them (0 to 1) that maximize b_i
                # For the objective function, we just sum their coefficients
                # In a real LP, these would be references to LP variables
                xd_var = lp_solver_variables.get(f'X_D_{task_x.id}_{q_id}_{v}', 0)
                xi_var = lp_solver_variables.get(f'X_I_{task_x.id}_{q_id}_{v}', 0)
                xp_var = lp_solver_variables.get(f'X_P_{task_x.id}_{q_id}_{v}', 0)

                if q_id in task_i.lr_resources:
                    b_l_i += (xd_var + xi_var + xp_var) * task_x.L_q[q_id]
                elif q_id in task_i.rr_resources:
                    b_r_i += (xd_var + xi_var + xp_var) * task_x.L_q[q_id]

    return b_l_i + b_r_i
key_insights: The objective function is a linear sum of blocking fractions multiplied by critical section lengths.
The `N_i_x_q` term is a crucial upper bound on interfering requests, linking the LP to the sporadic task model and response times.
This function is maximized by an LP solver subject to various constraints to find the worst-case blocking.

results.identifier: Constraint 1: Mutual Exclusivity of Delay Types

formal_description.statement: In any schedule of tau: For all tau_x in tau_i_prime, for all q, for all v: X_D_x_q_v + X_I_x_q_v + X_P_x_q_v <= 1.

variables.X_D_x_q_v: direct delay blocking fraction for R_x_q_v
variables.X_I_x_q_v: indirect delay blocking fraction for R_x_q_v
variables.X_P_x_q_v: preemption delay blocking fraction for R_x_q_v

assumptions: Definitions of direct, indirect, and preemption delay.
formal_description.conclusion: Ensures that a single request cannot simultaneously cause multiple types of pi-blocking for the task under analysis.

informal_sketch.intuition: A job can only be in one state at a time. It can't be directly waiting for a resource AND indirectly waiting for it AND be preempted all at the same instant by the same critical section. So, the sum of these blocking fractions for a single critical section cannot exceed 1 (meaning, it can't block for more than its own length).
steps: Recall the definitions of direct, indirect, and preemption delay.
Direct delay implies J_i has requested q and is suspended.
Indirect delay implies J_i has NOT requested q but is suspended due to a transitive dependency.
Preemption delay implies J_i implies J_i is NOT suspended but is preempted.
These states are mutually exclusive for J_i at any given time due to a single request R_x_q_v.
Therefore, the sum of their fractions cannot exceed 1.
key_insights: This constraint prevents overcounting of blocking time.
It's a fundamental sanity check for the LP model, ensuring physical impossibility is not modeled.

results.identifier: Constraint 2: No Preemption from Remote Agents (DPCP/DFLP)

formal_description.statement: In any schedule of tau under the DPCP or DFLP: For all tau_x in tau_i_prime, for all q in rr_tau_i, for all v: X_P_x_q_v = 0.

variables.rr_tau_i: set of remote resources for task tau_i
variables.X_P_x_q_v: preemption delay blocking fraction for R_x_q_v

assumptions: DPCP or DFLP protocols are used.
Definition of preemption delay (only agents executing on P_tau_i cause it).
formal_description.conclusion: States that preemption delay for task tau_i can only be caused by agents executing on tau_i's own processor, not by agents for remote resources.

informal_sketch.intuition: Preemption means a task is running on its processor and gets interrupted. If an agent is handling a resource on a *different* processor (a remote resource), it cannot directly preempt a task on *this* processor. So, remote agents don't cause preemption delay for the task under analysis.
steps: Identify resources that are remote to tau_i's processor (q in rr_tau_i).
Recall that preemption delay occurs when J_i is preempted on its own processor P_tau_i.
Agents for remote resources execute on their designated processors (P_q), not on P_tau_i.
Therefore, these remote agents cannot cause preemption delay for J_i on P_tau_i.
key_insights: This constraint leverages the partitioned nature of distributed protocols.
It eliminates a source of blocking, making the analysis less pessimistic.

dependencies: Definition: Objective Function for Total PI-Blocking

results.identifier: Constraint 3: Preemption Delay from Local, Lower-Priority Tasks (DPCP/DFLP)

formal_description.statement: In any schedule of tau under the DPCP or DFLP: sum(for all tau_x in tau_ll: sum(for v from 1 to N_i_x_q: X_P_x_q_v)) <= 1 + sum(for all u in rr_tau_i: N_i_u).

variables.tau_ll: set of local, lower-priority tasks for tau_i (tau_x | P_tau_x = P_tau_i AND x > i)
variables.N_i_x_q: max requests by tau_x for q while J_i is pending
variables.X_P_x_q_v: preemption delay blocking fraction for R_x_q_v
variables.rr_tau_i: set of remote resources for task tau_i
variables.N_i_u: max accesses by J_i to remote resource u

assumptions: DPCP or DFLP protocols are used.
Jobs issue at most one request at once.
formal_description.conclusion: Bounds the total preemption delay caused by local, lower-priority tasks for task tau_i, relating it to tau_i's own requests for remote resources.

informal_sketch.intuition: A lower-priority task on the same processor can only preempt tau_i if it gets a priority boost (e.g., by holding a lock) and tau_i is not suspended. This can happen once when tau_i is first released, and then each time tau_i suspends to wait for a remote agent and then resumes. So, the total number of times tau_i can be preempted by such tasks is limited to 1 (initial) plus the number of times it waits for remote agents.
steps: Identify local, lower-priority tasks (tau_ll).
These tasks can only issue requests (and thus potentially cause preemption delay) when tau_i is not scheduled.
This occurs when tau_i is waiting for a remote agent's response (i.e., suspended for a remote resource request).
J_i is released once, and waits at most `sum(N_i_u)` times for remote agents.
Each such waiting period is a chance for a local, lower-priority task to cause preemption delay.
Thus, the total preemption delay from such tasks is bounded by 1 (initial preemption) + `sum(N_i_u)` (preemptions after each remote wait).
key_insights: This constraint limits the number of times a lower-priority task can cause preemption delay.
It links preemption delay to the task's own remote resource requests, which involve suspension.

dependencies: Definition: Objective Function for Total PI-Blocking

results.identifier: Lemma 1: At Most One Request Delays (DFLP)

formal_description.statement: Let R_i_q_v denote a request of J_i, and let tau_x denote another task (tau_x != tau_i). At most one request of tau_x delays R_i_q_v.

variables.R_i_q_v: a specific request of job J_i for resource q
variables.R_x_u_w: a request of job J_x for resource u

assumptions: Jobs issue no more than one request at any time.
DFLP uses FIFO ordering for requests and agents.
formal_description.conclusion: Under DFLP, a single request of J_i can be delayed by at most one request from any other specific task tau_x.

informal_sketch.intuition: Because DFLP uses strict FIFO queues, if J_i's request is delayed by another task tau_x, it must be by an *earlier-issued* request from tau_x. Since tasks are sequential and only make one request at a time, tau_x can only have one such earlier-issued request that could be blocking J_i. Once that request is served, any subsequent request from tau_x would be *after* J_i's request and thus cannot delay it.
steps: Assume, for contradiction, that R_i_q_v is delayed by two requests from tau_x: R_x_u_w1 and R_x_u_w2.
Since tasks are sequential and issue one request at a time, if R_x_u_w2 delays R_i_q_v, it must have been issued *before* R_i_q_v.
However, if R_x_u_w1 also delays R_i_q_v, and R_x_u_w2 was issued after R_x_u_w1, then R_x_u_w2 would be served after R_x_u_w1.
Due to FIFO ordering, any request from tau_x that delays R_i_q_v must have been issued *before* R_i_q_v.
Since tau_x is sequential, it can have at most one such request pending or in progress that was issued before R_i_q_v.
Therefore, at most one request from tau_x can delay R_i_q_v.
key_insights: The FIFO property of DFLP is crucial here, simplifying blocking analysis.
This lemma significantly limits the number of interfering critical sections from any single task, reducing pessimism.

results.identifier: Constraint 4: Direct Request Delay under DFLP

formal_description.statement: In any schedule of tau under the DFLP: For all q, for all tau_x in tau_i_prime: sum(for v from 1 to N_i_x_q: X_D_x_q_v) <= N_i_q.

variables.N_i_x_q: max requests by tau_x for q while J_i is pending
variables.X_D_x_q_v: direct delay blocking fraction for R_x_q_v
variables.N_i_q: max accesses by J_i to q

formal_description.conclusion: Bounds the total direct request delay for task tau_i due to requests for a specific resource q from any other task tau_x, by the number of times tau_i itself accesses q.

informal_sketch.intuition: Direct delay only happens when J_i requests a resource q. If J_i requests q N_i_q times, it can be directly delayed by other tasks' requests for q at most N_i_q times. Lemma 1 says each of J_i's requests can be delayed by at most one request from any specific task tau_x. So, the total direct delay from all requests of tau_x for q cannot exceed the number of times J_i requests q.
steps: J_i can only incur direct delay for resource q if N_i_q > 0 (i.e., J_i actually requests q).
If J_i requests q, it does so N_i_q times.
Each of these N_i_q requests can be directly delayed by at most one request from any specific task tau_x (by Lemma 1).
Therefore, the sum of direct blocking fractions from all requests of tau_x for q cannot exceed N_i_q.
key_insights: This constraint directly applies Lemma 1 to direct blocking.
It limits the total direct blocking from a single interfering task for a specific resource, preventing overestimation.

results.identifier: Constraint 5: Direct and Indirect Delay under DFLP

formal_description.statement: In any schedule of tau under the DFLP: For all P_k, for all tau_x in tau_i_prime: sum(for all q in R_P_k: sum(for v from 1 to N_i_x_q: X_D_x_q_v + X_I_x_q_v)) <= N_i_P_k.

variables.R_P_k: set of resources local to processor P_k
variables.N_i_x_q: max requests by tau_x for q while J_i is pending
variables.X_D_x_q_v: direct delay blocking fraction for R_x_q_v
variables.X_I_x_q_v: indirect delay blocking fraction for R_x_q_v
variables.N_i_P_k: maximum number of requests by J_i for resources on processor P_k

formal_description.conclusion: Bounds the total direct and indirect request delay for task tau_i due to requests handled by a specific processor P_k from any other task tau_x, by the total number of times tau_i itself accesses resources on P_k.

informal_sketch.intuition: If J_i needs resources handled by processor P_k a total of N_i_P_k times, then it can be delayed (directly or indirectly) by other tasks' requests for resources on P_k at most N_i_P_k times. This is because each of J_i's requests can be delayed by at most one request from any specific task tau_x (Lemma 1).
steps: J_i can only be delayed by critical sections on processor P_k if N_i_P_k > 0 (i.e., J_i accesses at least one resource on P_k).
J_i makes N_i_P_k total requests for resources on P_k.
Each of these N_i_P_k requests can be delayed by at most one request from any specific task tau_x (by Lemma 1).
Therefore, the sum of direct and indirect blocking fractions from all requests of tau_x for resources on P_k cannot exceed N_i_P_k.
key_insights: This constraint extends the logic of Lemma 1 to cover both direct and indirect blocking for all resources on a given processor.
It provides a tighter bound by considering the total demand J_i places on a synchronization processor.

formal_description.statement: Under DPCP, agents in each cluster access resources on behalf of their clients according to the rules of the PCP. Crucial to the analysis of the DPCP is thus the set of resources with priority ceilings equal to or higher than the priority of J_i's agent. We let pc_tau_i = {q | exists tau_x such that x <= i and N_x_q > 0} denote the set of potentially conflicting resources. We further define pc_tau_i_P_k = pc_tau_i intersect R_P_k to denote the subset of potentially conflicting resources local to processor P_k.

variables.pc_tau_i: set of potentially conflicting resources for task tau_i
variables.x <= i: task tau_x has priority higher than or equal to tau_i
variables.N_x_q: max accesses by J_x to q
variables.pc_tau_i_P_k: subset of potentially conflicting resources local to processor P_k
variables.R_P_k: set of resources local to processor P_k

assumptions: Agent priorities correspond to task priorities.
PCP rules are applied for resource access.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the set of resources that can potentially cause blocking for task tau_i under DPCP, based on priority ceilings and resource locality.

informal_sketch.intuition: Under DPCP, a task tau_i can only be blocked by resources that are accessed by tasks with priority equal to or higher than itself (including itself). This set is `pc_tau_i`. `pc_tau_i_P_k` further filters this to only resources handled by a specific processor P_k.
steps: For each task tau_i, identify all resources q that are accessed by tau_i itself, or by any task tau_x with higher priority (x < i). This forms `pc_tau_i`.
Then, for each processor P_k, filter `pc_tau_i` to include only resources that are local to P_k. This forms `pc_tau_i_P_k`.
key_insights: The PCP's priority ceiling mechanism limits blocking to a specific set of resources.
This definition helps to exclude non-blocking resources from the analysis, reducing pessimism.

results.identifier: Constraint 6: No Direct/Indirect Delay from Non-Conflicting Resources (DPCP)

formal_description.statement: In any schedule of tau under the DPCP: For all tau_x in tau_i_prime, for all q not in pc_tau_i, for all v: X_D_x_q_v + X_I_x_q_v = 0.

variables.pc_tau_i: set of potentially conflicting resources for task tau_i
variables.X_D_x_q_v: direct delay blocking fraction for R_x_q_v
variables.X_I_x_q_v: indirect delay blocking fraction for R_x_q_v

assumptions: Agent priorities correspond to task priorities.
formal_description.conclusion: Under DPCP, task tau_i cannot incur direct or indirect request delay from resources that are not in its set of potentially conflicting resources.

informal_sketch.intuition: If a resource q is only accessed by tasks with priorities *lower* than tau_i, then any agent serving requests for q will have a lower effective priority than tau_i's agent. Therefore, tau_i's agent will always preempt or be served before agents for such resources, meaning tau_i won't be directly or indirectly delayed by them.
steps: Identify resources q that are not in pc_tau_i. By definition of pc_tau_i, these resources are only accessed by tasks with priorities strictly lower than tau_i.
Under DPCP, agent priorities correspond to task priorities.
Thus, any agent for such a resource q will have a lower effective priority than J_i's agent.
This implies J_i's agent will not be blocked by agents for q, meaning X_D_x_q_v = 0 and X_I_x_q_v = 0 for such q.
key_insights: This constraint leverages the priority ceiling mechanism of DPCP.
It significantly prunes the set of potential blocking sources, reducing pessimism.

results.identifier: Constraint 7: Ceiling Blocking Limit under DPCP

formal_description.statement: In any schedule of tau under the DPCP: For all P_k: sum(for all q in pc_tau_i_P_k: sum(for all tau_x where x > i: sum(for v from 1 to N_i_x_q: X_D_x_q_v + X_I_x_q_v))) <= N_i_P_k.

variables.pc_tau_i_P_k: subset of potentially conflicting resources local to processor P_k
variables.tau_x: any task with lower priority than tau_i (x > i)
variables.N_i_x_q: max requests by tau_x for q while J_i is pending
variables.X_D_x_q_v: direct delay blocking fraction for R_x_q_v
variables.X_I_x_q_v: indirect delay blocking fraction for R_x_q_v
variables.N_i_P_k: maximum number of requests by J_i for resources on processor P_k

assumptions: PCP limits ceiling blocking due to lower-priority jobs to one critical section per resource access by the higher-priority job.
formal_description.conclusion: Bounds the total direct and indirect delay for task tau_i from lower-priority tasks accessing resources on a specific processor P_k, by the number of times tau_i itself accesses resources on P_k.

informal_sketch.intuition: The PCP ensures that a higher-priority task (or its agent) can only be blocked by at most one critical section from a lower-priority task for each of its own resource requests. So, if J_i makes N_i_P_k requests for resources on processor P_k, it can be blocked by lower-priority tasks for resources on P_k at most N_i_P_k times in total.
steps: Consider J_i's requests for resources on processor P_k, totaling N_i_P_k requests.
For each of these requests, the PCP guarantees that J_i's agent will not be blocked by more than one critical section from a lower-priority task (x > i) for resources in pc_tau_i_P_k.
Therefore, the sum of direct and indirect blocking fractions from all lower-priority tasks (x > i) for resources on P_k cannot exceed N_i_P_k.
key_insights: This constraint directly applies the PCP's property of limiting ceiling blocking.
It provides a tight bound on blocking from lower-priority tasks, which is a common source of pessimism in other analyses.

dependencies: Definition: Objective Function for Total PI-Blocking

formal_description.statement:
W_i_q denotes a bound on the maximum wait time of J_i when requesting q. W_i_q = W_L_i_q + W_H_i_q + L_i_q.

W_L_i_q = max({L_x_v | x > i AND v in pc_tau_i_P_q} union {0}) is the maximum direct and indirect request delay caused by lower-priority tasks.

W_H_i_q = sum(for all tau_x where x < i: ceil((r_x + W_i_q) / p_x) * sum(for all y in pc_tau_i_P_q: N_x_y * L_x_y)) is the higher-priority 'demand' for resources on processor P_q, solved iteratively.

D_x_y_i_q = ceil((r_x + W_i_q) / p_x) * N_x_y is the maximum number of requests for a resource y issued by jobs of a task tau_x during the interval that a single request of J_i for resource q remains incomplete.

variables.W_i_q: maximum wait time of J_i when requesting q
variables.W_L_i_q: maximum direct/indirect delay from lower-priority tasks for J_i's request for q
variables.W_H_i_q: maximum direct/indirect delay from higher-priority tasks for J_i's request for q
variables.L_i_q: maximum critical section length for q by J_i
variables.L_x_v: critical section length for resource v by task tau_x
variables.x > i: task tau_x has lower priority than tau_i
variables.pc_tau_i_P_q: subset of potentially conflicting resources local to processor P_q
variables.x < i: task tau_x has higher priority than tau_i
variables.N_x_y: max accesses by J_x to y
variables.L_x_y: max critical section length for y by tau_x
variables.D_x_y_i_q: max requests for y by tau_x during J_i's request for q

assumptions: Response-time analysis can be applied to individual requests.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines components of the maximum wait time for a single resource request under DPCP, which are used to bound blocking from higher-priority tasks.

informal_sketch.intuition: When J_i requests a resource q, it might have to wait. This total wait time (W_i_q) is its own critical section length (L_i_q), plus any blocking from lower-priority tasks (W_L_i_q), plus any blocking from higher-priority tasks (W_H_i_q). W_L_i_q is simply the longest critical section of a lower-priority task that could block it. W_H_i_q is calculated iteratively, like a mini-response time analysis for the request itself. D_x_y_i_q then uses this W_i_q to figure out how many times a higher-priority task tau_x could access resource y while J_i's request for q is pending.
steps: Calculate W_L_i_q: Find the maximum L_x_v among all lower-priority tasks (x > i) accessing resources in pc_tau_i_P_q.

Calculate W_H_i_q iteratively: Start with W_H_i_q = 0. In each iteration, sum up the demand from higher-priority tasks (x < i) for resources in pc_tau_i_P_q, using the current W_i_q (which includes W_H_i_q). Repeat until W_H_i_q converges.
Calculate W_i_q = W_L_i_q + W_H_i_q + L_i_q.
Calculate D_x_y_i_q using the converged W_i_q, which estimates how many jobs of tau_x can interfere with J_i's request for q.
key_insights: This is a per-request response time analysis, providing a tighter bound than whole-job analysis.
It accounts for both lower- and higher-priority interference during a single critical section.
The iterative calculation for W_H_i_q is similar to standard response time analysis but applied to a shorter interval.

results.identifier: Constraint 8: Direct/Indirect Delay from Higher-Priority Tasks (DPCP)

formal_description.statement: In any schedule of tau under the DPCP: For all y, for all tau_x where x < i: sum(for v from 1 to N_i_x_y: X_D_x_y_v + X_I_x_y_v) <= sum(for all q in R_P_y: N_i_q) * D_x_y_i_q.

variables.tau_x: any task with higher priority than tau_i (x < i)
variables.N_i_x_y: max requests by tau_x for y while J_i is pending
variables.X_D_x_y_v: direct delay blocking fraction for R_x_y_v
variables.X_I_x_y_v: indirect delay blocking fraction for R_x_y_v
variables.R_P_y: set of resources local to processor P_y
variables.N_i_q: max accesses by J_i to q
variables.D_x_y_i_q: max requests for y by tau_x during J_i's request for q

assumptions: W_i_q and D_x_y_i_q are accurately calculated.
formal_description.conclusion: Bounds the total direct and indirect delay for task tau_i from higher-priority tasks accessing a specific resource y, by the total number of times tau_i accesses resources on y's processor multiplied by the maximum number of times tau_x can access y during one of tau_i's requests.

informal_sketch.intuition: When J_i requests any resource q on processor P_y, that request remains incomplete for at most W_i_q time. During this interval, a higher-priority task tau_x can make at most D_x_y_i_q requests for resource y. Since J_i makes `sum(N_i_q)` requests for resources on P_y, the total direct/indirect blocking from tau_x for resource y is limited by `sum(N_i_q) * D_x_y_i_q`.
steps: For each resource y and higher-priority task tau_x, calculate D_x_y_i_q, which is the maximum number of times tau_x can access y while J_i's request for q is pending.
J_i makes `sum(N_i_q)` requests for resources on processor P_y (where resource y is located).
Each of these requests can be delayed by tau_x's requests for y.
Therefore, the total sum of direct and indirect blocking fractions from tau_x for resource y is bounded by the product of J_i's total requests on P_y and D_x_y_i_q.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def add_constraint_dpcp_higher_priority_delay(lp_solver, blocking_fraction_vars, task_i, task_set, resource_map, D_x_y_i_q_map, processor_map):
    for y_id in resource_map.keys():
        P_y_id = resource_map[y_id].assigned_processor
        sum_Ni_q_on_Py = task_i.calculate_N_P_k(P_y_id, processor_map)

        for task_x in task_set:
            if task_x.priority >= task_i.priority: continue # Only higher priority tasks (x < i)
            
            sum_xd_xi_x_y_v = 0
            N_i_x_y_coeff = math.ceil((r_values[task_i.id] + r_values[task_x.id]) / task_x.p) * task_x.N_q.get(y_id, 0)
            for v in range(1, int(N_i_x_y_coeff) + 1):
                sum_xd_xi_x_y_v += lp_solver.get_variable(f'X_D_{task_x.id}_{y_id}_{v}') + \
                                   lp_solver.get_variable(f'X_I_{task_x.id}_{y_id}_{v}')
            
            # D_x_y_i_q is specific to J_i's request for q, but the constraint sums over all q in R_P_y
            # The paper's formula uses D_x_y_i_q, which is derived for a *single* request of J_i for *any* q.
            # This implies D_x_y_i_q is a general bound for any of J_i's requests on P_y.
            # So, we use the D_x_y_i_q calculated for task_i and resource y.
            D_x_y_i_q_val = D_x_y_i_q_map[task_x.id][y_id] # Assuming this map is passed in

            lp_solver.add_constraint(sum_xd_xi_x_y_v <= sum_Ni_q_on_Py * D_x_y_i_q_val)
key_insights: This constraint is crucial for bounding blocking from higher-priority tasks, which can be a major source of pessimism.
It leverages the per-request response time analysis (W_i_q) to provide a much tighter bound on interfering requests.
It ensures that only relevant higher-priority requests are considered, not all possible requests.
